chapters.title: 1 Background
chapters.summary:
David Ogilvy recounts his unconventional path to advertising: born in England in 1911, educated at Fettes and Oxford, then thrown out, followed by years as a chef at the Hotel Majestic in Paris, a door-to-door salesman of AGA cooking stoves in Scotland (where he wrote his celebrated sales manual for AGA), and a researcher at the Gallup organization in America studying polling and audience research.

During World War II he worked for British intelligence in Washington. After the war he bought a farm in Pennsylvania among Amish neighbors before founding the agency Hewitt, Ogilvy, Benson & Mather in New York in 1948 with no clients and a staff borrowed largely from London. His early breakthroughs came fast: Schweppes with Commander Whitehead's beard, Rolls-Royce's 'at 60 miles an hour the loudest noise comes from the electric clock,' and Dove soap positioned as not drying your skin. He built the agency on research discipline learned at Gallup rather than showmanship.
chapters.takeaway: Diverse experience—selling, research, writing—compounds into an edge; ground creativity in facts about customers.

chapters.title: 2 How to Manage an Advertising Agency
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy distills management principles honed while building his agency into one of the world's largest. He insists managers set exalted standards: 'If you always hire people who are smaller than you, we shall become a company of dwarfs. If you always hire people who are bigger than you, we shall become a company of giants.' He advocates hiring superior talent, delegating authority, and letting subordinates shine.

He covers practical disciplines: run meetings efficiently, write clear memoranda, make decisions promptly, and never tolerate second-rate work because it demoralizes first-rate people. He urges managers to know their people personally, praise publicly while criticizing privately, and maintain an atmosphere of civilized informality. He warns against office politics and empire-building, favoring flat structures where great creative work outranks hierarchy. His model is the craftsman-manager who stays close to the product—an ad man who still writes ads—not an administrator detached from the agency's output.
chapters.takeaway: Hire people better than yourself, delegate boldly, and enforce high standards without crushing morale.

chapters.title: 3 How to Get Clients
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy describes how a new agency wins accounts when it starts with none. His tactics included courting prospects through published expertise—the famous agency 'house ads' and his own speeches and books functioned as bait—plus relentless preparation for pitches. He landed Seagram's, Shell, and General Foods by demonstrating knowledge of their businesses that exceeded incumbents'.

He advises researching the prospect thoroughly, presenting ideas specific to their problems rather than generic brilliance, and being honest about weaknesses since candor disarms skepticism. He notes luck's role: timing, referrals from satisfied clients, and publicity from early campaigns like Schweppes created momentum. He counsels against chasing every account—some clients aren't worth having—and against pitching business you can't serve well. Above all, he stresses that new business is won by showing, in the pitch itself, advertising so good it proves your competence beyond argument.
chapters.takeaway: Win clients by demonstrating deep knowledge of their business and presenting brilliant work in the pitch itself.

chapters.title: 4 How to Keep Clients
chapters.summary:
Keeping clients, Ogilvy argues, depends less on brilliant advertising than on managing relationships. He kept clients like Shell and American Express for decades by making them feel secure: no surprises, constant communication, and visible results measured in sales. He advises telling clients bad news yourself before they hear it elsewhere, and never letting them be ambushed.

He details practices: keep the top man informed directly, socialize with clients' leadership, understand their politics, and give them credit for successes. He warns agencies lose accounts through arrogance, neglect after winning, or letting junior staff handle senior relationships. He also acknowledges limits—when a client demands work that violates professional standards, an agency should resign rather than compromise, as he did when clients pushed him too far. The underlying principle: treat the client's money as if it were your own, and they will trust you with more of it.
chapters.takeaway: Keep clients through candor, constant communication, measurable results, and treating their money like your own.

chapters.title: 5 How to Be a Good Client
chapters.summary:
Flipping perspective, Ogilvy instructs advertisers on getting the most from their agencies. Good clients select an agency carefully and then back it decisively; he cites Unilever and General Foods as exemplary clients whose discipline produced consistently strong advertising. He urges clients to brief agencies thoroughly—complete market facts, strategy, and ambitions—and then resist meddling with creative execution.

He tells clients to demand research-based justification rather than personal taste, to judge campaigns against objectives, and to avoid committee approval processes that sand off distinction ('a camel is a horse designed by a committee'). He warns against changing agencies impulsively, squeezing fees until quality suffers, or hiring multiple agencies on the same brand to play them against each other. Pay agencies fairly and promptly, share long-term plans, and reward risk-taking. The best advertising emerges from mutual trust between a decisive client and a confident agency.
chapters.takeaway: Brief thoroughly, decide decisively, pay fairly, and resist committees that turn bold ideas into camels.

chapters.title: 6 How to Build Great Campaigns
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy lays out his campaign philosophy: 'Unless your campaign contains a big idea, it will pass like a ship in the night.' A great campaign rests on positioning—what the product does and for whom—as with Dove's 'for dry skin' and Volkswagen's honest 'Think Small.' He insists on committing to one positioning and staying with it for decades, citing Marlboro Country and Commander Whitehead's Schweppervescence.

He prescribes concrete rules: present the consumer's problem and how the product solves it, include news and information because consumers crave facts, use headlines that deliver the whole selling message, and never run an advertisement you wouldn't want your own family to see repeatedly. He champions research-tested claims over empty superlatives, argues twenty years of consistent image-building beats flashy one-offs, and warns against change for its own sake. Campaigns succeed through repetition of a single powerful idea, not novelty per execution.
chapters.takeaway: Find one big positioning idea, commit to it for decades, and let repetition compound your brand.

chapters.title: 7 How to Write Potent Copy
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy treats copywriting as a craft with learnable rules. Headlines matter most—they do the heavy lifting, so promise a benefit, include the brand name, and test alternatives; five times as many people read headlines as body copy. Write the headline first, then lead with a strong first paragraph that pays off the promise.

His stylistic commandments: write the way you talk, use short words and sentences, avoid jargon and superlatives ('great,' 'amazing'), stick to the facts because specifics sell—'At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise comes from the electric clock' outsells any adjective. Use testimonials, especially from real users; cite numbers; tell stories. Edit ruthlessly—he rewrote headlines dozens of times, producing 19 drafts of the Rolls-Royce ad. Never use more than a few typefaces, keep paragraphs short, and end copy on the strongest point. Research first: 'Advertising people who ignore research are as dangerous as generals who ignore decodes of enemy signals.'
chapters.takeaway: Write fact-rich, conversational copy with benefit-driven headlines, and edit relentlessly until it sings.

chapters.title: 8 How to Illustrate Advertisements and Posters
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy explains visual persuasion: pictures must attract the right reader and communicate instantly, so use photographs that arouse curiosity—his famous eye-patch man for Hathaway shirts made a shirt brand iconic through story appeal. Illustrations should relate directly to the headline's promise; gratuitous cleverness wastes attention. Show the product in use whenever possible, and feature before-and-after demonstrations which remain among the most persuasive formats.

For posters, simplicity is absolute: one idea, readable at speed, memorable at a glance—Ogilvy cites his Schweppes posters showing the bottle with Commander Whitehead. He gives technical guidance: caption under photographs gets read more than body text, retain consistent art direction across a campaign so ads are recognizable, and avoid clutter. Test visuals against each other where possible. The picture's job is not decoration but amplification of the selling message, working in seamless partnership with headline and copy.
chapters.takeaway: Use photos with story appeal that amplify the headline, keeping posters brutally simple and recognizable.

chapters.title: 9 How to Make Good Television Commercials
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy applies direct-response discipline to television: the commercial exists to sell, not to entertain. He catalogs proven formats—product demonstration (the American Tourister luggage gorilla), talking-head presentations, slice-of-life dramas, testimonials, and problem-solution structures—ranking demonstration highest because it shows the claim being true.

He urges advertisers to state the brand name early and often, since viewers forget; to show the package prominently; to open with a strong hook because viewers flee within seconds; and to repeat key claims. He warns against commercials so entertaining viewers remember the joke but not the product, mocking award-chasing 'creative' work that fails to move goods. Music and gimmicks must serve comprehension. He advises testing commercials the same way print ads are tested, and staying with winners: a commercial that keeps selling shouldn't be retired for boredom—viewers tire of ads far later than agencies do.
chapters.takeaway: Make commercials that sell—demonstrate the product, name it often, and don't retire what works.

chapters.title: 10 How to Rise to the Top of the Tree
chapters.summary:
Addressed to young advertising professionals, this chapter maps ambition. Ogilvy advises mastering the fundamentals—learn to write, to sell, and to understand research—before seeking glory. Ambition should express itself in doing exceptional work rather than maneuvering for titles: 'big shots are only little shots who keep shooting.'

He recommends choosing the right agency and mentor, volunteering for hard assignments, and becoming indispensable through sheer usefulness. Specialize in what you love, but understand the whole business. Cultivate habits of industry: he famously worked long hours and expected others to find work they loved enough to labor at it joyfully. He warns against job-hopping for small raises, cynicism, and coasting. Success in advertising, as in his own career, comes from combining craftsmanship with courage—presenting bold, researched ideas and defending them against timid committees until excellence itself becomes your reputation.
chapters.takeaway: Rise by mastering fundamentals and doing fearless, excellent work—little shots become big shots by continuing to shoot.

chapters.title: 11 Things I Hope to Find in Young People
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy lists the qualities he sought when hiring, drawn from decades of building his agency's staff. High on the list: honesty and integrity, since advertising handles clients' fortunes; intelligence combined with common sense; and the capacity for hard work sustained over years. He values originality and a restless imagination, but tempered by discipline—ideas mean nothing without the persistence to execute them.

He looks for people with wide interests beyond advertising, good manners, and the humility to accept criticism and learn from research. He prizes enthusiasm bordering on obsession, resilience in the face of rejection (most ideas die in client meetings), and the ability to get along with colleagues while remaining independent-minded. He admits he hired misfits and eccentrics when they were brilliant, preferring gifted irregulars to polished mediocrity. The portrait that emerges: a curious, industrious, truthful person who loves the work more than the perks.
chapters.takeaway: Hire for integrity, curiosity, and obsessive love of the work—brilliant eccentrics beat polished mediocrity.

chapters.title: Can Advertising Sell Everything?
chapters.summary:
In his closing reflection, Ogilvy confronts the moral reach of his profession. He believes advertising can sell almost anything that genuinely serves the buyer—from soap to candidates to charitable causes—and cites campaigns for public health and conservation as proof of advertising's constructive power. Persuasion, honestly done, informs choice rather than corrupting it.

But he draws lines: advertising cannot sustainably sell products that disappoint, because truth surfaces through experience and word of mouth eventually destroys false promises. He expresses pride in what advertising accomplished—raising living standards by creating mass markets, funding free media—and disdain for its abuses, including deceptive claims and pandering to the lowest instincts. He closes with characteristic confidence in research-guided, information-rich advertising as both commercially effective and socially defensible, urging practitioners to treat their power seriously and to refuse work that would embarrass them if exposed.
chapters.takeaway: Advertising can sell nearly anything true and useful—but never sustainably sell what betrays the customer.
